summary: Chogye Trichen was a scholar in Tibetology and Buddhist studies who studied under traditional teacher Thubten Gyatso. Around 1932 to 2007, he served as the Eighteenth Chogye Trichen at Nalendra Monastery.
Active in Tibetology and Buddhist studies, Chogye Trichen Rinpoche studied under traditional teachers Geshe Tshechok (1929), Kunga Chophel, and Zimwok Rinpoche.
Chogyū Takayama worked in philosophy and Japanology. He was educated at Fukushima Prefectural Asaka High School and studied at the University of Tokyo from circa 1894 to 1897.
Chokgyur Dechen Lingpa was a figure in Tibetology and Buddhist studies. He studied under traditional teachers Jamyang Khyentse Wangpo and Jamgön Kongtrul Lodrö Thaye, whom he also taught.

A Buddhist studies and Tibetology scholar, Chokyi Nyima Rinpoche studied at Young Lamas Home School, Rumtek Monastery, and under teachers including the 16th Karmapa and Khenchen Thrangu Rinpoche. He became abbot of Ka-Nying Shedrub Ling in 1976.
Chong Go is a Buddhist studies scholar who studied at Dongguk University and trained under traditional teacher Daehaeng (attested 2012).
Chris Clark specializes in Buddhist studies and Indology. He completed a PhD under Mark Allon at the University of Sydney by 2015 and served as an honorary associate there, attested in 2019.

Christian August Brandis worked in philosophy and history and archaeology, studying at Kiel University (~1808–1812). He held posts at the University of Copenhagen (~1812–1815), Humboldt University of Berlin (~1815–1821), and the University of Bonn (~1821–1867).

Christian Bartholomae was an Iranian, Central Asian, linguistics, and Indology scholar who studied under Heinrich Hübschmann. He held posts at Halle-Wittenberg (~1885–1890), Giessen (~1890–1898), Münster (~1898–1900), and Heidelberg (~1909–1925).

Christian Bernert is a Tibetology and Buddhist studies scholar who studied at the International Buddhist Academy and the University of Vienna under Klaus-Dieter Mathes, Junjie Chu, Karin Preisendanz, and Gerald Hödl.

Christian Coseru studied at the University of Bucharest and completed his PhD at the Australian National University (~1999–2003) under John Powers and Jay L. Garfield. His posts include Associate Professor of Philosophy at the College of Charleston (~2006).

Christian Gottlob Heyne was a linguistics and history/archaeology scholar who studied at Leipzig University (1748–1752). In 1763, he became a professor at the University of Göttingen, where he also directed the library from 1764 to 1812.

Christian Haskett is an Indology, Buddhist studies, and Tibetology scholar who completed his PhD at the University of Wisconsin-Madison (attested 2010), advised by Robert A. F. Thurman and Michael Chamberlain. He held a post at Washington and Lee University.

Christian K. Wedemeyer studied at Columbia University (PhD 1999 under Robert A. F. Thurman). A scholar of Buddhist studies, religious studies, and Indology, he taught at the University of Copenhagen (2000–2003) before joining the University of Chicago around 2003.

Christian Karl Josias von Bunsen studied at Marburg, Göttingen under Christian Gottlob Heyne, Munich, Leiden, and Copenhagen, and under Antoine-Isaac Silvestre de Sacy. He was active in religious studies and linguistics and founded the German Archaeological Institute in 1829.

Christian Lassen studied at Oslo, Heidelberg, and Bonn (PhD ~1823–1827 under August Wilhelm Schlegel). Specializing in Indology and linguistics, he held posts at the University of Bonn as Privatdozent (1830) and professor of ancient Indian language and literature (1840–1876).

Christian Lee Novetzke studied at Macalester College, Harvard, and Columbia University (PhD ~1996–2003). Specializing in Indology, religious studies, and history/archaeology, he taught at the University of Pennsylvania (2003–2007) and became a professor at the University of Washington in 2007.

Christian Lindtner was a scholar of Buddhist studies and Indology who completed his doctorate at the University of Copenhagen by 1982. He served as a professor at the University of Copenhagen, attested between 1980 and 1991.

Christian Luczanits earned his Magister and PhD at the University of Vienna. A scholar in Buddhist studies, Tibetology, and Indology, he has been a visiting professor at Stanford and UC Berkeley, and served as curator at the Rubin Museum of Art (attested 2012).

Christian Wittern specializes in sinology and Buddhist studies and studied under Seizan Yanagida. He has held posts at Kyoto University (attested 1993 and 2008) and Hanazono University (attested 2011).
